title: Memory-like innate response to booster vaccination with MF-59 adjuvanted influenza vaccine in children.
ehr_evidence: The study used prospectively collected peripheral blood samples for transcriptomics, flow cytometry, and HAI assays in a randomized clinical trial (NCT02529904); no electronic health record, claims, or registry data were used.
summary: A randomized clinical trial (NCT02529904) of MF59-adjuvanted trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine in 90 children aged 15-24 months and 30 young healthy adults, using systems-level transcriptional, flow cytometry, and antibody analyses to characterize memory-like innate immune responses to prime and booster vaccination.
key_findings: Booster vaccination induced a stronger transcriptional response with 221 genes passing significance cutoffs (FDR < 0.05 and fold-change > 1.5), nearly three times the number of upregulated genes compared with prime vaccination.
Elevated type 1 interferon response post-booster vaccination correlated with local reactogenicity (early-onset erythema and swelling) in toddlers.
Baseline interferon-signing transcriptional signature correlated with downstream hemagglutinin inhibition (HAI) antibody titers.
We found no transcriptional or cellular correlates of fever (systemic reactogenicity).
Strong and significant increase in the activation marker CD40 on all monocyte subsets at days 1 and 3 post boost, indicating enhanced memory-like innate response.
No significantly up- or down-regulated genes at the pre-boost baseline (day 28) compared with pre-prime baseline (day 0) at the gene level.
captured_features: Peripheral blood gene expression (transcriptomics, Affymetrix HG-133plus2.0 chips)
Flow cytometry monocyte/myeloid cell subsets and CD40 expression
Gene set enrichment analysis blood transcriptional modules (BTMs)
pathologies_diseases: Vaccine reactogenicity (local adverse effects: erythema, swelling, fever)
study_design: Randomized controlled clinical trial (prime-boost design with staggered cohort sampling)
population: 90 children aged 15-24 months and 30 young healthy adults (25-40 years)
limitations: Staggered sample collection design due to limits on blood draws from children, with cohorts B and C lacking pre-vaccination baseline.
Small cohort sizes and healthy-volunteer sampling may limit generalizability.
No transcriptional correlates of systemic reactogenicity (fever) were identified.
